summary: Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare (CRUSH) Proposed Rule (CMS-6098-P) On Nov. 16, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a proposed rule that would strengthen program integrity (PI) oversight and the agency's ability to prevent, identify, and address fraud, waste, and abuse across Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), and the Health Insurance Marketplace. The Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare (CRUSH) proposed rule is a standalone, discretionary rule rather than an annual payment rule. It proposes changes to provider and supplier enrollment requirements; Medicare Advantage (MA) and Medicare Part D oversight; Medicaid and CHIP program integrity and eligibility oversight; Medicare durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS) supplier requirements; and Marketplace agent and broker oversight. CMS intends to conduct program integrity rulemaking of this kind on an annual basis going forward. Background On Feb. 27, 2026, CMS issued a Request for Information (RFI) (91 FR 9803) seeking public input on regulatory changes that could help the agency more effectively prevent, identify, and address fraud, waste, and abuse and protect taxpayer dollars across its programs. CMS received over 560 comments and suggestions in response to the RFI, some of which informed the provisions of this proposed rule. This proposed rule supports Administration priorities on program integrity oversight, including the June 6, 2025, Presidential Memorandum on Eliminating Fraud, Waste, and Abuse in Medicaid, and Executive Order 14395, which established the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud. Medicare Provider Enrollment and Oversight Faster Reporting of Enrollment Changes Under current regulations, providers and suppliers generally have 30 calendar days to report critical changes to their Medicare enrollment information (such as changes in practice location, ownership, or adverse legal actions) and up to 90 calendar days to report other types of changes. CMS is proposing to require that all providers and suppliers report any change to their enrollment information within 30 calendar days, regardless of the type of change or the type of provider or supplier involved. CMS believes this accelerated timeline will improve the agency's ability to prevent, identify, and address fraud, waste, and abuse. New Grounds for Medicare Enrollment Denial and Revocation CMS is proposing to add a new ground for denial or revocation that would apply when a provider or supplier has a domestic or foreign owner, managing employee, organization, partner, officer, or director whose identity cannot be confirmed, or whom CMS determines poses an undue risk of fraud, waste, and abuse. CMS believes this new authority would help prevent bad actors from enrolling in, or remaining in, the Medicare program. Medicare Advantage and Part D Program Integrity Mandatory Fraud, Waste, and Abuse Reporting CMS currently encourages, but does not require, MA organizations and Part D plan sponsors to report referrals of substantiated or suspicious fraud, waste, and abuse. In addition, CMS requires reporting of inappropriate prescribing of opioids and payment suspensions for pharmacies based on credible allegations of fraud but does not require reporting of payment suspensions based on credible allegations of fraud for other provider or supplier types. For calendar year 2025, CMS determined, through its review of a frequency report, only 46% of Medicare Part C and Part D plan contracts voluntarily reported referrals of substantiated or suspicious fraud, waste, and abuse to CMS and only 19% of Medicare Part C and Part D plan contracts reported any payment suspensions based on credible allegations of fraud to CMS, including both pharmacies and other provider and supplier types. CMS is proposing to make referrals by MA organizations and Part D plan sponsors to CMS of substantiated or suspicious fraud, waste, and abuse mandatory and to expand MA organization and Part D plan sponsor reporting of payment suspensions based on credible allegations of fraud by pharmacies to all provider and supplier types. This proposal is also consistent with a July 2018 Office of Inspector General (OIG) recommendation that CMS require plan sponsors to report Part C and D fraud and abuse incidents and corrective actions to a centralized system. Medicare Advantage Provider Enrollment in Fee-for-Service Medicare Current regulations do not generally require providers and suppliers who bill MA plans to also be enrolled in Original Medicare. CMS currently relies on a preclusion list as an alternative screening mechanism, but this list operates reactively, after a provider has already begun billing MA plans, rather than screening providers before they begin furnishing services. CMS is proposing to add a requirement, at proposed § 422.222(a), that all eligible providers and suppliers billing MA be enrolled in Original Medicare in an approved status except for Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) plans. This would allow CMS to apply its full Original Medicare enrollment screening process, including identity verification, licensure review, site visits, and fingerprint-based background checks, to providers and suppliers participating in MA. If finalized, this requirement would take effect on the first day of the plan year beginning two years after publication of the final rule. Risk Adjustment Data Validation (RADV) Program Reforms The MA RADV program is CMS' primary way to address overpayments to MA organizations by identifying when there is a lack of documentation in the medical record to support the diagnoses reported for risk adjustment. Specifically, CMS is proposing to codify that it would not apply a fee-for-service (FFS) adjuster, would determine the applicable sampling methodology, and would begin extrapolation of audit findings with payment year (PY) 2018 audits. CMS estimates that this approach would enable the agency to collect an average of approximately $9 billion per payment year in MA program overpayments. RADV Hardship Exception Process Currently, the process for granting a hardship exception for medical record submission during a RADV audit exists only in sub-regulatory guidance, without a formal regulatory framework. CMS is proposing to establish a regulatory framework identifying the extraordinary circumstances that would qualify a plan sponsor for a hardship exception, which CMS expects would improve the consistency and transparency of hardship exception determinations. Medicare DMEPOS Program Integrity Declining Bonds from Noncompliant Sureties CMS currently lacks authority to decline a DMEPOS surety bond from a surety company that has previously failed to fulfill its financial obligations to CMS. CMS is proposing a new regulation, modeled on 31 C.F.R. § 223.17(b)(1), establishing a process by which CMS may decline bonds from noncompliant sureties, to protect the Medicare Trust Funds. DMEPOS Supplier Affiliation Reporting DMEPOS suppliers are currently required to report owners with a 5% or greater interest, general and limited partners, managing employees, and corporate officers and directors on the Form CMS-855S Medicare enrollment application. CMS is proposing to expand this disclosure requirement to include additional associated entities, such as companies that furnish marketing, fulfillment, wholesale, or device manufacturing services to the supplier. CMS believes this expanded disclosure would help expose interrelated fraudulent network operations. Redefining “Sufficient Evidence” for Surety Bond Liability Current regulations (42 C.F.R. § 424.57(a)) define “sufficient evidence” of surety bond liability, but CMS has found that sureties frequently claim the evidence provided is insufficient to avoid their payment obligations. CMS is proposing to revise this definition to include greater detail as to what constitutes “sufficient evidence.” CMS believes this would reduce sureties' ability to avoid their financial obligations. Expanding the Prohibition on Unsolicited Beneficiary Contact Current regulations (42 C.F.R. § 424.57(c)(11)) prohibit DMEPOS suppliers from contacting beneficiaries by telephone without prior permission, subject to limited exceptions, but this prohibition does not extend to email, text messages, social media, or door-to-door contact. CMS is proposing to expand this prohibition to also cover text messages and add new § 424.57(c)(31) to address social media direct messages, email without an opt-out feature, and door-to-door solicitation, subject to the same exceptions that currently apply to telephone contact. CMS believes this expanded protection would better protect beneficiaries from high-pressure marketing and fraudulent solicitation schemes. Medicaid and CHIP Program Integrity Reliance on Credible Allegation of Fraud (CAF) Determinations Under current regulations (42 C.F.R. § 455.23), a state Medicaid agency must suspend payments to a provider upon determining that a credible allegation of fraud (CAF) exists, unless good cause exists not to suspend. CMS cannot currently trigger a state's obligation to make this determination directly. CMS is proposing to allow states to rely on a CAF determination made by CMS or by another federal agency to establish their own CAF finding under § 455.23(a)(1)(i). CMS is also proposing to narrow the "good cause" exception at § 455.23(e). A state is not required to rely on another agency's CAF determination; where a state disagrees with a determination CMS has made, CMS encourages the state to engage with CMS' Center for Program Integrity to better understand the basis for CMS' determination. State Fraud and Abuse Reporting Requirements Current regulations (42 C.F.R. § 455.17), issued in 1978 and amended in 1983, require states to report suspected provider fraud and abuse complaints that warrant full investigation, using six specified data elements. CMS is proposing to add new required data elements, including a provider's National Provider Identifier (NPI), address and location, and all actions taken against the provider, under § 455.17(b)(6). CMS believes existing requirements no longer provide sufficient detail to support effective national oversight, trend analysis, or coordination between CMS and its state partners. Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) Enhancements The 21st Century Cures Act requires states to implement EVV systems for personal care services (PCS) and home health (HH) services, but current regulations do not require states to use EVV data as part of prepayment claims review or preliminary fraud, waste, and abuse investigations. CMS is proposing to modernize these requirements to require that states incorporate EVV information into Medicaid prepayment review activities and preliminary investigations, strengthening oversight in these historically high-risk service areas. National Provider Identifier Requirements for All Eligible Provider Types Under current regulations (42 C.F.R. Part 455, Subpart E), states are not required to consistently collect, maintain, or use NPIs across all eligible Medicaid and CHIP provider types, systems, and activities. CMS is proposing to require states to collect, maintain, and use NPIs for all eligible Medicaid and CHIP providers across enrollment, revalidation, claims processing, managed care oversight, program integrity, and reporting activities, consistent with 45 C.F.R. Part 162. CMS believes this would improve the ability of both states and CMS to prevent, identify, and address fraud, waste, and abuse at the individual provider level.
